segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: SECTION 1: SOCIAL DIALOGUE

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You will hear a conversation between a student, Anna, and her friend, Ben, about a volunteering event.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: Ben, have you got a minute? I'm trying to organise the volunteering day for the community centre, and I need a second opinion.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Sure. What's the problem?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: Well, it's not exactly a problem. We've got three possible dates, and I can't decide which one to choose. The first is Saturday the 12th of April.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: The 12th? That's the same weekend as the town football final, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: Is it? I didn't know that. That might be a problem, because a lot of the volunteers are football fans.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Actually, wait. I think the final is on the 13th, not the 12th. Let me check... yes, the 13th. So the 12th should be fine.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: Good. The second date is Saturday the 19th of April.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: That's the start of the school holidays. Some people will be away.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: That's what I thought. And the third is Saturday the 26th.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: The 26th is after the holidays, so people should be back. But isn't that the day of the library book sale?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: The book sale is on the 25th, I think. Let me look at the notice... yes, the 25th. So the 26th is free.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Then I'd choose the 26th. It gives people time to come back from holiday, and it doesn't clash with the football or the book sale.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: That makes sense. Now, the second thing: we need to decide what the volunteers will actually do. Last year we painted the hall, but this year the hall has already been painted.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: What about the garden? The back garden is in a terrible state.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: True. But we'd need tools, and we'd need someone who knows about plants.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: My neighbour is a gardener. She might help. But she's away until the 20th.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: That's fine if we choose the 26th. Could you ask her?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Yes, I'll ask her tomorrow. What else needs doing?

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: The kitchen needs cleaning, and the notice board needs repairing. The notice board is probably a one-person job.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: I can do the notice board. I'm not very good at cleaning kitchens.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: Perfect. So we'll do the garden, the kitchen and the notice board. How many volunteers do we need?

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: For the garden, maybe six. For the kitchen, three. And one for the notice board. So ten in total.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: Last year we had fourteen, so ten should be manageable. I'll put a sign-up sheet in the hall.

segments.speaker: Ben
segments.text: Good idea. And I'll ask my neighbour about the garden tools.

segments.speaker: Anna
segments.text: Thanks, Ben. You've been a great help.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: SECTION 2: SOCIAL MONOLOGUE

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You will hear a talk given by a museum volunteer, Claire, to a group of new visitors.

segments.speaker: Claire
segments.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Marlow Bridge Museum. My name is Claire, and I'm one of the volunteers here. Before you start looking around, I'd like to give you a short introduction to the museum and to explain a few practical things.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: The museum opened in 1987, in a building that was originally a school. The school closed in 1975, and for a few years the building was empty. Then a group of local people raised money to turn it into a museum. We now have about 4,000 objects, although only about 800 are on display at any one time. The rest are kept in storage.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: The museum is arranged over two floors. On the ground floor, you'll find the local history gallery, which covers the period from 1800 to 1950. This includes tools, clothes, photographs and a reconstruction of a fisherman's kitchen. On the first floor, we have the temporary exhibition space. At the moment, the exhibition is about the sea wall, which some of you may have read about in the newspaper. It includes photographs of the old wall and maps of the proposed new design.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: A few practical points. The museum is free to enter, but we welcome donations. There are donation boxes near the entrance and in the first-floor gallery. The café is on the ground floor, next to the shop. It serves hot drinks, sandwiches and cakes, and it closes at 4:30, half an hour before the museum closes. The toilets are on both floors. There is a lift near the main stairs, and it is available for anyone who needs it.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Photography is allowed, but please do not use a flash in the galleries, because the light can damage some of the objects. If you are visiting with children, there is a small activity area on the first floor with books and drawing materials. We also run a free guided tour at 11 o'clock every morning, which lasts about 45 minutes. You don't need to book; just meet at the entrance.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, I should mention that the museum is run almost entirely by volunteers. If you are interested in helping, even for a few hours a month, please speak to me or pick up a leaflet at the desk. We need people to help in the shop, to welcome visitors and to help with school groups. No experience is necessary, and we provide training.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Thank you, and I hope you enjoy your visit.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: SECTION 3: ACADEMIC DISCUSSION

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You will hear a discussion between two students, Maria and Tom, and their tutor, Dr Lewis, about a research project on memory and evidence.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: So, Maria, Tom, you've been working on your project about memory and evidence. How is it going?

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: Quite well, I think. We've collected most of our data, but we're having some trouble interpreting it.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: Tell me more.

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: Well, we interviewed twenty people about a short film they had watched. We asked half of them one set of questions and half another set. We expected the two groups to give similar answers, but they didn't.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: The group that was asked about the speed of the car gave much higher estimates than the other group.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: That's interesting. Why do you think that happened?

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: At first I thought it was because the two groups were different in some way. But then I checked, and they were similar in age and background.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: So we think the wording of the question affected their answers.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: That's a reasonable interpretation. But before you conclude that, what else should you consider?

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: We should consider whether the film was clear enough. If the film was blurry, people might have guessed.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: Good. And what about the order of the questions?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: We didn't think about that. We asked the speed question first in both groups.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: So the order was the same. That's helpful, because it means the difference is less likely to be due to order. But you should still mention it as a limitation.

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: We will. We're also worried about the sample size. Twenty people is quite small.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: Yes, it is. You can't generalise from twenty people. But for a student project, it's acceptable if you are honest about the limitations. What are you planning to do next?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: We're going to write up the results and then compare them with the published studies we read.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: Good. And remember to separate what you observed from what you think it means. Your observations are the answers people gave; your interpretation is that the wording affected them. Keep those two things distinct in your report.

segments.speaker: Maria
segments.text: That's helpful. We were also thinking of adding a question about confidence, asking people how sure they were.

segments.speaker: Dr Lewis
segments.text: That's a good idea. It might show whether confidence and accuracy are related. But don't be surprised if they are not strongly related. Many studies find that confidence is a poor guide.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: We'll add it. Thank you, Dr Lewis.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: SECTION 4: ACADEMIC LECTURE

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You will hear part of a lecture on urban accessibility and the fifteen-minute city.

segments.speaker: Lecturer
segments.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to discuss the idea of the fifteen-minute city, and in particular the role of evidence in making it work.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: The fifteen-minute city is a model in which residents can reach most daily services within a fifteen-minute walk or cycle ride. The idea has become popular in recent years, but it is not entirely new. Many older neighbourhoods were built before cars became common, and they already contain shops, schools and clinics within a short distance. What is new is the attempt to measure accessibility systematically.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, measuring accessibility is not as simple as it sounds. You have to decide which services count. Does a fifteen-minute city need a hospital, or is a clinic enough? You also have to decide what 'close enough' means. Is it distance, travel time or cost? And you have to consider the quality of the route. A supermarket may be only 500 metres away, but if a busy road with no crossing separates it from a neighbourhood, the distance is short but the accessibility is poor.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: For this reason, some planners use a walkability score. This score includes pavement width, crossing points, street lighting and traffic speed. A simple map of distances can therefore mislead, because it ignores these factors.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Critics of the model raise several concerns. First, the model may suit wealthy city centres better than suburbs or rural areas, where services are naturally more spread out. Second, improving one neighbourhood can raise rents and push lower-income residents elsewhere. This process is sometimes called green gentrification. Third, focusing on walking distance may neglect people with disabilities, older residents and those who need to carry heavy shopping. A fifteen-minute city that works only for healthy adults is not a fifteen-minute city for everyone.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Supporters respond that the model is a direction, not a fixed rule. The aim is to reduce unnecessary car journeys and to make streets safer, not to force everyone to walk. They also point out that accessibility can be improved without building new shops. A frequent bus service, a safe crossing or a covered bicycle park can make existing services easier to reach.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Let me give you an example from a simulated project in the town of Riverton. Planners there added two pedestrian crossings and a small bus stop. The measured walking time to the nearest clinic fell from twenty-two minutes to fourteen minutes, without any new building. They also surveyed 600 residents and recorded journey times at different hours. They found that the average resident could reach a pharmacy in nine minutes but a hospital in thirty-five minutes. They found that residents without cars relied heavily on two bus routes, and that these routes stopped running after 7 p.m. This evidence led the council to fund an evening bus service rather than to build a new health centre, because the bus service addressed a more immediate problem at lower cost.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: So the fifteen-minute city is best understood as a method for asking better questions: Who can reach which services, how, and at what cost? The answers will differ from place to place. A model that ignores local evidence may produce attractive maps but poor decisions. A model that uses local evidence carefully can help communities identify the smallest changes that make the largest difference.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: In the next lecture, we will look at how to design a survey and how to avoid common errors in collecting evidence. Thank you.
